analogy.p: Imagine delivering water energy through a long pipe. Pushing a large flow of water at low pressure through the pipe causes lots of friction and wastes energy as heat. If the same energy is carried as a high-pressure, low-flow stream, there is much less friction, so less energy is wasted. Here the pressure is the p.d., the flow rate is the current and friction is the cable's resistance. The analogy breaks down because friction in a pipe does not depend on the square of the flow in the same simple way, and electrical energy is not carried by the charge itself but by the electric field and the p.d. that drives it.

bullets: The Grid is a network: **power stations** (gas, nuclear, wind, solar, biomass, hydroelectric and others) feed electrical power into it, and **consumers** (homes, businesses, industry) take power out of it.
Its main parts are **cables** (overhead on pylons or underground) and **transformers**; the spec wording is 'a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers'.
Electrical **power** is transferred (not 'electricity is made at the plug'); power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W), so the Grid delivers energy per second.
Because many different power stations are connected, the Grid can keep supply matched to demand: when demand rises, more stations or stored energy can be brought on.
The Grid uses **alternating current (a.c.)**, because only a.c. can be stepped up and down by transformers.
Link to energy resources: any resource that generates electricity (fossil fuels, nuclear, renewables) connects to the same Grid.
Key exam phrase: the Grid is an **efficient** way to transfer energy because it uses a high p.d. and so a low current in the cables.
core.h: What the National Grid is and what it does
core.p: The **National Grid** is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers. It lets electrical power made at many different power stations be shared out across the whole country, so that homes, schools, hospitals and factories everywhere can draw the power they need at any time. Without it, every town would need its own power station and a surplus in one place could not help a shortage in another. The key idea for the exam is that the Grid moves electricity at a very **high potential difference (p.d.)** because that is the efficient way to do it.

bullets: Stage 1: **generator** at the power station produces a.c. at a relatively modest p.d. (tens of thousands of volts).
Stage 2: **step-up transformer** raises the p.d. to as much as 400 000 V (400 kV) for the long-distance transmission lines.
Stage 3: **transmission cables** (overhead on pylons) carry the electrical power across the country at high p.d. and low current.
Stage 4: **step-down transformers** at substations reduce the p.d. in steps (for example to tens of thousands of volts, then to a few thousand volts for local distribution).
Stage 5: a final **step-down transformer** near homes reduces the p.d. to **230 V**, the safe(r) value for domestic use.
The total power (energy per second) delivered is almost the same at each stage; what changes is the split between p.d. and current.
Step-up transformers are located near the power station; step-down transformers are located nearer the consumers. Mixing these up is a very common error.
core.h: The journey from power station to home
core.p: Electricity follows a set route. A generator at the power station produces an alternating p.d. (typically around 25 000 V). This is fed into a **step-up transformer**, which increases the p.d. to a very high value, up to about 400 000 V on the main transmission lines. The electricity then travels along the cables, usually on pylons, over long distances. Near towns and cities it reaches a substation containing a **step-down transformer**, which reduces the p.d. in stages, and a final step-down transformer reduces it to the 230 V a.c. used in homes.

bullets: The UK domestic mains is **230 V a.c.** at **50 Hz** (both values are in the specification and are worth learning exactly).
In a.c. the p.d. keeps changing direction, so the current in a circuit continually reverses; in d.c. the current is always in the same direction.
The 230 V quoted is the effective (rms-type) value; you only need to know it as the standard domestic p.d.
The p.d. in a mains-supplied house is much lower than in the transmission lines (400 000 V) because 400 kV would be extremely dangerous and impossible to insulate in a home.
A lower p.d. in the home is safer, though 230 V is still dangerous, which is why plugs have fuses and earth wires.
Frequency 50 Hz means 1 cycle takes 1/50 = 0.02 s (period = 1 / frequency).
Link to Electricity topic: mains safety uses the live, neutral and earth wires; the Grid is the supply that feeds them.
core.h: Mains supply in the UK: 230 V and 50 Hz
core.p: The mains electricity in UK homes is an **alternating current (a.c.)** supply with a frequency of **50 hertz (Hz)** and a p.d. of about **230 V**. Alternating current means the direction of the current repeatedly reverses, 50 complete cycles every second. This is different from direct current (d.c.), like that from a cell or battery, which flows in one direction only. The Grid is built around a.c. because transformers, which are needed to change p.d. efficiently, only work with a changing (alternating) current.

bullets: **P = V I**: power (W) = potential difference (V) x current (A). Rearranged: I = P / V and V = P / I.
**P = I² R**: power (W) = current² (A²) x resistance (ohms, Ω). This gives the power wasted as heat in a resistor, such as a cable.
Because the current is squared, the power wasted is proportional to **I²**: doubling the current makes the loss four times bigger; halving it makes the loss a quarter.
Power is the rate of energy transfer: 1 W = 1 J per second, so 1 kW = 1000 W and 1 MW = 1 000 000 W.
The equation E = P t gives the energy transferred (J) from power (W) and time (s).
Always convert units first: kV to V (x 1000), MW to W (x 1 000 000), before substituting.
Link to Electricity topic: the same two equations appear in the calculations on energy transfers in appliances.
core.h: Power, potential difference and current: the key equations
core.p: To understand why the Grid works the way it does you need two equations. The first is the **power** equation, **power = potential difference x current** (P = V I), where power is in watts (W), p.d. in volts (V) and current in amperes (A). The second is the **heating power** equation, **power = current squared x resistance** (P = I² R). Together they explain the whole idea: for a fixed amount of power delivered, raising the p.d. lowers the current, and a lower current wastes far less energy as heat in the cable's resistance.

bullets: Resistance comes from collisions between moving electrons and the lattice ions of the metal.
The energy transferred in these collisions heats the cable: this is the **heating effect of a current**, and it is wasted energy.
The wasted power is **P = I² R**, so it depends on the cable's resistance R and the current I.
The cable resistance depends on length (longer = more resistance), cross-sectional area (thicker = less resistance), and material.
Wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings and cannot be usefully recovered, which lowers the efficiency of the whole system.
Because a power station cannot make up for large wasted energy cheaply, the Grid is designed to reduce losses as far as possible.
Link to Electricity topic: this is the same heating effect that makes a kettle element or toaster glow, except in the Grid it is unwanted.
core.h: Why energy is lost in the cables
core.p: Every cable has some **resistance**. When a current flows through a resistor, charge carriers (electrons) collide with the ions in the metal lattice. These collisions transfer energy to the thermal energy store of the cable, so the cable heats up and the energy is **dissipated** to the surroundings as wasted thermal energy. The longer the cable, the more resistance it has, and across a whole country the cables are hundreds of kilometres long, so the wasted energy could be very large unless it is kept down.

bullets: For a fixed power P, I = P / V, so **higher V gives lower I**.
Wasted power = I² R, so a **lower current** means **much less** energy is wasted as thermal energy in the cables.
The loss falls as the square of the current: current / 10 means loss / 100.
Worked comparison: 20 MW through a 10 Ω cable at 25 kV wastes 6.4 MW; at 400 kV it wastes only 25 kW (see worked examples).
Full mark-scheme chain: step-up transformer increases p.d. -> for the same power, current is decreased -> less energy is dissipated (as heat) in the cables -> more efficient.
The resistance of the cable does not change when the p.d. changes; it is the **current** that is reduced.
Never say 'higher voltage means less resistance' or 'the voltage pushes less energy out' - the mark is for lower current.
core.h: Why a high p.d. makes transmission efficient
core.p: This is the central idea. The power delivered along a cable is P = V I. If the same power must be transmitted, then raising the **p.d. V** means the **current I** must be smaller (I = P / V). Because the power wasted as heat is P = I² R, a smaller current reduces the loss enormously. Increasing the p.d. by a factor of 16 reduces the current by a factor of 16 and the wasted power by a factor of 16² = 256. So stepping up the p.d. makes the Grid an **efficient** way of transferring energy, because far less energy is wasted as heat in the cables.

bullets: Thicker cables lower resistance R but are heavy, expensive and need stronger supports.
Using a high p.d. and a low current is the cheaper way to reduce I² R losses.
Overhead cables are insulated from the pylons by large ceramic or glass insulators, and run high above the ground so that people and vehicles are safe.
A very high p.d. is dangerous: it can cause sparks through air (arcing), so the lines are kept a safe distance away from people.
Underground cables are safer and hidden from view but cost much more and are harder to repair, so most long-distance lines are overhead.
The Grid design is a compromise: lower losses versus cost, safety and appearance.
Evaluation answers should mention **cost** and **safety** as well as efficiency.
core.h: Why not just use thicker cables or a low p.d.?
core.p: You might ask why the Grid does not reduce losses another way, for example by using very thick, low-resistance cables. A thicker cable has less resistance, but it needs much more metal (usually copper or aluminium), is heavier, costs far more and needs stronger pylons. Raising the p.d. is much cheaper because transformers are very efficient and need little maintenance. There is also a limit to how high the p.d. can go, since the cables must stay well insulated and clear of the ground, so the Grid is a **compromise** between cost, safety and efficiency.

bullets: **Step-up transformer**: more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, so the output p.d. is greater than the input.
**Step-down transformer**: fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil, so the output p.d. is less than the input.
Step-up transformers are positioned at the **power station**; step-down transformers are at **substations** and near homes.
Increasing p.d. means a lower current for the same power; decreasing p.d. means a higher current in the final distribution.
Transformers work only with **a.c.**, which is why the Grid uses alternating current.
Transformers are very efficient (often over 99%), so little energy is wasted in the transformers themselves.
The electrical power output of an ideal transformer equals the power input.
core.p: A **transformer** changes the p.d. of an alternating supply. A **step-up transformer** increases the p.d. and is used at the power station end, and a **step-down transformer** decreases the p.d. and is used near consumers. In the Grid, step-up transformers raise the p.d. before transmission so that the current is low, and step-down transformers reduce the p.d. to a much lower, safer value (230 V) for domestic use. Transformers cannot make energy: if the p.d. goes up, the current goes down, so the power stays almost the same.

bullets: Primary coil: input; secondary coil: output; both wound on a **soft iron core** (the core is not connected electrically to either coil).
An a.c. in the primary makes a **changing magnetic field** in the core; the core carries this field through the secondary coil.
The changing magnetic field induces an alternating p.d. across the secondary coil (electromagnetic induction).
A direct current gives a steady magnetic field, which does not change, so **no p.d. is induced** in the secondary: transformers do not work on d.c.
Transformer equation: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns** (p.d. across primary / p.d. across secondary = turns on primary / turns on secondary).
For a 100% efficient transformer: **Vs x Is = Vp x Ip** (power out = power in), so a larger p.d. in the secondary means a smaller current in the secondary.
The transformer equations are Higher tier calculations; the descriptions of step-up and step-down are for everyone.
Link to Magnetism and electromagnetism: this uses the same induction effect as a generator, where a changing magnetic field induces a p.d.
core.h: How a transformer works (Physics only content)
core.p: A transformer has two coils of insulated wire, the **primary coil** and the **secondary coil**, wound around a **soft iron core**. An alternating p.d. across the primary coil makes an alternating current, which creates a **changing magnetic field** in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil and, by electromagnetic induction, **induces an alternating p.d.** across the secondary coil. The size of the output p.d. depends on the number of turns on each coil, and an iron core is used because it is easily magnetised and so carries the changing magnetic field from one coil to the other.

bullets: Method: write the equation, rearrange for the unknown, substitute with SI units, calculate, state the unit.
Vs = Vp x Ns / Np and Ns = Np x Vs / Vp (rearranged forms).
Turns ratio Ns / Np = Vs / Vp; if the ratio is greater than 1, it is a step-up transformer.
Ip = Vs Is / Vp (rearranged from power in = power out).
Check your answer: a step-up transformer must give a bigger p.d. and a smaller current; a step-down transformer gives a smaller p.d. and a bigger current.
If a question says the transformer is not 100% efficient, power out is less than power in; use efficiency = useful power out / total power in.
Units: p.d. in volts, current in amps; turns are just numbers with no units.
core.h: Using the transformer equations (Higher tier calculations)
core.p: For a transformer, the ratio of p.d.s is equal to the ratio of the numbers of turns: **Vp / Vs = Np / Ns**. If the secondary has more turns than the primary, the output p.d. is bigger and it is a step-up transformer. If it has fewer, it is a step-down transformer. For a transformer that is 100% efficient, the electrical power output equals the electrical power input: **Vs Is = Vp Ip**. So if the p.d. is stepped up by a factor of 16, the current must be stepped down by a factor of 16, which is exactly why the Grid keeps the current in the transmission lines low.

bullets: Transformers need a **changing** magnetic field, so they need a.c. input.
Step-up transformers allow efficient long-distance transmission; step-down transformers make the supply safe for use.
Generators in power stations naturally produce a.c. as the coil rotates in a magnetic field.
The mains frequency is 50 Hz in the UK, so the direction reverses 100 times per second (twice per cycle).
The fact that the mains is a.c. also affects domestic safety design, such as the live and neutral wires.
Link to Magnetism and electromagnetism: induction in generators and transformers uses the same physics.
Exam statement: 'Transformers only work on a.c.' is a frequently-tested fact.
core.h: Why the Grid uses a.c. and why this matters
core.p: Because transformers only work on alternating current, the Grid is an a.c. system. A d.c. supply could not easily be stepped up or down using transformers, and the energy lost in long cables at low p.d. would be far greater. Alternating current also allows a generator to be a simple rotating coil in a magnetic field, giving a naturally alternating output. The combination of **a.c., transformers and high p.d.** is what makes long-distance electrical power transfer practical and cost-effective.

bullets: The cables are suspended from **insulators** on pylons so charge cannot flow through the pylon into the ground.
They are high above the ground so people, animals and vehicles cannot touch or get dangerously close.
Overhead lines are cheaper and easier to repair but are unsightly and can be damaged by storms.
Underground cables avoid the visual impact but are more expensive and harder to repair.
A warning sign on a pylon, a fence around a substation and a locked door are safety features for the very high p.d.
Large power stations are often built near sources of fuel or cooling water, which is why a national transmission system is needed.
Link to Energy resources: the choice of where to build power stations is separate from where people live; the Grid solves this by connecting them.
core.h: Overhead cables, safety and the environment
core.p: Most long-distance transmission lines are **overhead cables** hung from tall pylons. Overhead cables are cheaper to build and maintain than underground cables, but they are visible and can be damaged by weather. Underground cables are hidden and safer but cost much more. Because the p.d. on the lines is extremely high, the cables are kept far from the ground and from people, and are held away from the metal pylons by insulators so that the electricity does not flow through the pylon to the ground.

bullets: Demand varies with time of day and season; the Grid manages this by increasing or reducing the power fed in.
Some power stations respond quickly to demand (for example gas and hydroelectric), while others take hours to start (for example some coal and nuclear).
**Pumped storage**: use surplus electrical energy to pump water uphill, then release it through turbines when demand is high.
Wind and solar output varies with the weather, so the Grid needs other sources or storage to cover shortfalls.
Link to Energy resources: reliability, cost and environmental impact all feed into which stations feed the Grid.
Link to Electricity: P = VI, P = I²R, E = Pt, and E = QV are used with Grid data.
Link to Magnetism and electromagnetism: induction explains both generators and transformers.
core.h: Matching supply and demand, and linking to other topics
core.p: The demand for electricity changes during the day and the year: it is higher in the evening and in winter, and lower overnight. The National Grid connects many power stations so that supply can be matched to demand. Some power stations (like gas) can be switched on quickly, while others (like nuclear) provide a steady base supply. Surplus energy can be stored, for example by pumping water uphill in a pumped-storage hydroelectric scheme, and released at times of high demand. The Grid also connects to wind and solar generation, whose output depends on the weather.

exam: **Command words**: 'Explain why' wants a chain of reasoning (cause then effect), 'Describe' wants what happens in order, 'Calculate' wants working and units, 'Evaluate' wants both sides and a judgement.

**Efficiency of the Grid (typically 3-4 marks)**: (1) step-up transformers increase the p.d.; (2) for the same power, the current is lower (P = V I); (3) less energy is wasted as heat in the cables (P = I squared R); (4) so the transmission is more efficient.
**Location of transformers (1-2 marks)**: step-up at the power station; step-down near homes or at substations; give the purpose of each.
**Why a.c.?** Transformers need a changing magnetic field so only work with a.c.; a d.c. would give no induced p.d. in the secondary.
**Calculation marks**: usually 1 for the correct equation or rearrangement, 1 for substitution (with converted units) and 1 for the answer with a unit.
**Learn the values**: UK mains is 230 V a.c. and 50 Hz; Grid transmission up to about 400 000 V (400 kV).
**Transformer equation (Higher)**: Vp / Vs = Np / Ns; Vs Is = Vp Ip. Show the rearrangement before substituting.
**Graph questions**: if shown a graph of power loss against current it is a curve (parabola) because loss is proportional to I squared; do not draw a straight line.
**6-mark questions**: a good answer links p.d. up, current down, heating down, efficiency up, mentions transformers on a.c., and gives step-down for safety; use full sentences with because and so.
**Avoid** vague words such as 'energy is lost' without saying where it goes: always say 'dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings'.

mistakes.r: The resistance of the cable stays the same. A high p.d. means a lower current (I = P / V), so less energy is dissipated as heat.
mistakes.w: A high voltage reduces the resistance of the cables, so less energy is wasted.

mistakes.r: Step-up transformers are at the power station; step-down transformers are near the consumers.
mistakes.w: The step-up transformer is near the houses.

mistakes.r: Transformers only work with a.c. because a changing magnetic field is needed to induce a p.d. in the secondary coil.
mistakes.w: Transformers work with direct current as well as a.c.

mistakes.r: Energy is conserved. If the p.d. goes up, the current goes down; power out cannot be greater than power in.
mistakes.w: A transformer creates extra energy because the voltage goes up.

mistakes.r: A lower current means less energy wasted as heat (P = I squared R), so transmission is more efficient.
mistakes.w: The higher the current, the more efficient the transmission.

mistakes.r: The transmission lines are at up to about 400 000 V; 230 V is the domestic mains supply.
mistakes.w: Electricity is transferred at 230 V along the pylons.

mistakes.r: Power wasted = I squared R, so halving the current reduces the power wasted to one quarter.
mistakes.w: Halving the current halves the power wasted.

mistakes.r: Convert to base units first: 1 kV = 1000 V and 1 MW = 1 000 000 W, otherwise the answer is wrong by factors of a thousand.
mistakes.w: Use kV and MW straight in P = V I.

summary: You need to know that the National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers, that step-up transformers raise the p.d. for transmission and step-down transformers lower it to 230 V for homes, and why this makes energy transfer efficient (a higher p.d. means a lower current and less heating in the cables). It matters because it is a standard 4 to 6 mark explanation question, and it uses P = V I and P = I² R, plus the transformer equations in Higher tier.

terms.d: A system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
A device that changes the potential difference of an alternating supply, using two coils wound on an iron core.
A transformer that increases the potential difference; it has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.
A transformer that decreases the potential difference; it has fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts (V).
The rate of flow of charge; measured in amperes (A).
The rate of energy transfer; measured in watts (W); P = V I.
A measure of how hard it is for charge to flow through a component; measured in ohms (Ω).
A current that repeatedly changes direction; UK mains is 50 Hz.
A current that flows in one direction only.
The number of complete cycles per second; measured in hertz (Hz). UK mains is 50 Hz.
Energy that is spread out to the surroundings (usually as thermal energy) and is not useful.
useful energy (or power) output divided by total energy (or power) input.
The production of a potential difference across a conductor when it is in a changing magnetic field.
The input coil of a transformer, connected to the supply.
The output coil of a transformer, in which the output potential difference is induced.

worked.ans: (a) 6.4 MW wasted (32% of the 20 MW); (b) 25 kW wasted (0.125% of the 20 MW). The higher p.d. gives a much smaller current, so far less energy is wasted.
worked.q: 20 MW of power is transmitted through cables with a total resistance of 10 ohms. Calculate the power wasted as heat when the power is transmitted at (a) 25 000 V and (b) 400 000 V. [6 marks]
steps: Power wasted = I squared x R = 800² x 10 = 640 000 x 10 = 6 400 000 W = 6.4 MW.
Power wasted = 50² x 10 = 2500 x 10 = 25 000 W = 25 kW.
Check: the p.d. is 16 times larger, the current is 16 times smaller (800 / 16 = 50) and the loss is 16² = 256 times smaller (6 400 000 / 25 000 = 256).

worked.q: A step-up transformer has 2000 turns on its primary coil and 32 000 turns on its secondary coil. The input p.d. is 25 000 V and the input current is 160 A. Assume the transformer is 100% efficient. Calculate (a) the output p.d. and (b) the output current. [5 marks]
steps: (a) Vp / Vs = Np / Ns, so Vs = Vp x Ns / Np.
(b) For 100% efficiency: Vs Is = Vp Ip, so Is = Vp Ip / Vs.
Check: p.d. x 16, current / 16, so the power is unchanged: 25 000 x 160 = 4.0 MW and 400 000 x 10 = 4.0 MW.

worked.ans: Full-mark answer: A step-up transformer increases the p.d., so for the same power the current in the cables is lower. The thermal energy wasted in the cable's resistance is P = I² R, so a lower current means much less energy is dissipated, making transmission more efficient. Step-down transformers then reduce the p.d. to 230 V for safe domestic use.
worked.q: Explain why electricity is transmitted across the country at a very high potential difference. [4 marks]
steps: Mark 1: A step-up transformer increases the p.d. of the supply before transmission.
Mark 2: For the same power (P = V I), a higher p.d. means a lower current in the cables.
Mark 3: The energy wasted as heat depends on the current squared (P = I² R), so a lower current means less energy is dissipated as thermal energy in the cables.
Mark 4: This makes the transmission more efficient (and cheaper), and step-down transformers then reduce the p.d. to a safe 230 V for homes.
